catalog_quote: Le shiwa est une langue à tons. Il utilise donc les variations de la hauteur de la voix pour distinguer les ‘’mots’’. Le ton est généralement associé à un support vocalique. En shiwa, il peut être associé à des consonnes nasales utilisées comme indice de classe et à des voyelles. [...] [p.174] En shiwa, quatre tons ont une valeur distinctive: le ton haut, le ton bas, le ton montant et le ton descendant. Les tons modulés ne sont pertinents que sur les lexèmes monosyllabiques. Dans les autres cas, seuls les tons hauts et bas sont pertinents. [...] L’analyse montre que quatre paramètres conditionnent la réalisation des tons dans le lexème: 1) La position: Dans les lexèmes polysyllabiques, la position initiale est une position rehaussante et la position finale, une position abaissante. En position finale, le ton haut est réalisé moyen, soit sous l’effet d’une consonne abaissante, soit sous l’effet d’un ton bas.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Shiwa is a tone language. It therefore uses variations in voice pitch to distinguish 'words'. Tone is generally associated with a vocalic support; in Shiwa it can be associated with nasal consonants used as class markers and with vowels. [...] In Shiwa four tones are distinctive: high, low, rising and falling. The contour tones are relevant only on monosyllabic lexemes. [...] 1) Position: in polysyllabic lexemes the initial position is a raising position and the final position a lowering position.
new_statements.citation: Ollomo Ella, Régis. 2013. Description linguistique du shiwa, langue bantu du Gabon : phonologie, morphologie, syntaxe, lexique. Thèse de doctorat, Université Sorbonne Nouvelle – Paris 3 (HAL tel-01130996).
new_statements.locator: Part 'Phonétique et phonologie', ch.3 'Système tonal', p.145 (opening) and §3.4 'Conclusion', p.174
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (PDF + extracted text of Ollomo Ella 2013, Dougere 2007; scanned txt of Puech 1989; present and accurate). QUOTE: In the opening of ch.3 'Systeme tonal' is on PDF page 145 (printed 145; TOC also gives 145): 'Le shiwa est une langue a tons. Il utilise donc les variations de la hauteur de la voix pour distinguer les mots. Le ton est generalement associe a un support vocalique. En shiwa, il peut etre associe a des consonnes nasales utilisees comme indice de classe et a des voyelles.' -- verbatim. Sec. 3.4 'Conclusion' on p.174: 'En shiwa, quatre tons ont une valeur distinctive : le ton haut, le ton bas, le ton montant et le ton descendant. Les tons modules ne sont pertinents que…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shiwa is described purely as a tone language (H, L, and rising/falling contours on monosyllables; six phonetic levels/contours across three registers). The most complete description (317-pp. thesis with a 35-page tone chapter and instrumental F0 data) has no notion of word stress or accent at all; the only positional asymmetry it reports is tonal register (lexeme-initial syllable realised on a raised register, lexeme-final on a lowered one). A shorter earlier sketch (Dougère 2007: 48-49) remarks in passing that V2/word-final stem vowels reduce or elide because they are 'dénuée d'accent … dans une position faible', implying stem-initial prominence, but no source states an accent-placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Dougère 2007 (pp.48-49) is the only text using the word 'accent': non-initial (V2, final) mid-open vowels centralise or drop 'quand la voyelle est dénuée d'accent et donc située dans une position faible', more often in young speakers; nominal prefixes are always low-toned (Dougère p.84) and the syllabic nasal prefix bears L (Ollomo Ella p.175).
new_statements.domain_note: Ollomo Ella's tonal analysis is on the lexème (stem/word in citation form, from recorded wordlists, with Praat F0 figures); positional raising/lowering refers to lexeme-initial vs lexeme-final syllables. No phrase-level prominence discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same variety: Shiwa/ʃíwə́ (self-name of speakers bèʃíwə́), also written chiwa (Dougère 2007), ʃiwə (Puech 1989), 'makina'/'fang makina', Osyeba/Ossyeba; spoken around Booué, Ogooué-Ivindo, Gabon; Guthrie/Maho A803, Makaa-Njem (A80), closest to Kwasio/Ngumba; Glottolog shiw1234, no ISO code (xiw proposed 2025). Not to be confused with Puech 1990 'Upstep in a Bantu tone language' (Pholia 5), which is on li-Duma/li-Wanji (B50) and was saved in the folder only because of a citation ambiguity (flagged).

new_statements.quote: [p.192] Dans son mémoire, Ollomo Ella relève trois registres de tons — H, B et M — donnant lieu à cinq tons grâce à des modulations. Il reconnaît plusieurs niveaux de tons M mais ne retient que deux tons phonologiques : H et B. Sa thèse apportera sans doute une réponse plus développée. À ce jour, les deux études mènent à la conclusion que le shiwa comporte deux tonèmes de base — H et B — et des schèmes comme H, B, BH et HB. [p.193, Tableau 28] Tons — Registres H, B, M — Tonèmes H, B
new_statements.translation: [p.192] In his master's thesis, Ollomo Ella notes three tone registers — H, L and M — giving rise to five tones through modulations. He recognises several levels of M tone but retains only two phonological tones: H and L. His doctoral thesis will no doubt give a more developed answer. To date, the two studies lead to the conclusion that Shiwa has two basic tonemes — H and L — and schemes such as H, L, LH and HL. [p.193, Table 28] Tones — Registers H, L, M — Tonemes H, L

The same section also gives Dougère's four simple realisations (H, B…
new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement from Ollomo Ella 2013 (tone language, no stress statement): Cheucle's Shiwa sketch is a synthesis of Puech 1989, Dougère 2007/2010 and Ollomo Ella 2008 (explicitly excludes Ollomo Ella's 2013 thesis) and reaches the same two-toneme (H, B) analysis with no mention of stress. It adds nothing that would fill the catalog's empty rule field; it confirms 'tonal, stress unstated'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shiwa is presented as a tone language with two tonemes (H, B/L) and lexical tone schemes H, B, BH, HB (plus phonetic M and a falling 'B+' in final position per Dougère); the thesis contains no statement about word stress, accent or prominence anywhere (zero hits for accent / proéminence / stress / tonique / emphase in both extracted text extraction modes over all 642 pages). The only 'prosodic' remarks (pp.481, 516: the C2 position is 'prosodiquement faible') concern consonant erosion in second-syllable position across A80, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. On tone: Dougère's M and 'B+' (falling low) tones occur only in final position and are not retained in transcription; modulated tones HB/BH occur only in monosyllabic bases, attributed to tone reassociation after final-vowel elision (p.192); low tone on syllabic nasal class prefixes that is lost in the plural (p.192).
new_statements.identity_note: Cheucle's Shiwa sketch (pp.176-193) is based on Dougère (2007, 2010), Puech (1989) and Ollomo Ella (2008), all describing the Shiwa spoken at Booué and surroundings, Ogooué-Ivindo province, Gabon (p.176: 'Les travaux sus-cités portent sur le shiwa parlé à Booué et ses alentours'). Cheucle's own fieldwork was on Bekwel, not Shiwa.

sources.note: Part 'Phonétique et phonologie' pp.81-180; ch.3 'Système tonal' pp.145-174 treats Shiwa as a tone language (six phonetic tone realisations on three registers; four tonemes H, L, rising, falling, contour tones distinctive only on monosyllables). No section, term or statement on word accent/stress anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent: 'accent' occurs only in unrelated senses and in a bibliography title). Only positional remark is tonal-register: in polysyllabic lexemes initial position raises and final position lowers tone realisation (p.174).

sources.citation: Dougère, Lucie. 2007. Première approche phonologique, morpho-syntaxique et diachronique du chiwa du Gabon (Ogooué-Ivindo). Mémoire de Master 2, Université Lumière Lyon 2. 211 pp.
sources.note: Ch.2 §5 'Tons' pp.79-85: tone only (H, B, plus M and extra-low B+ as word-final lowered realisations; two contour tones), nominal prefixes always L. No accent rule; the single accent remark is pp.48-49: mid-open vowels in V2 centralise, and word-finally may centralise or elide 'quand la voyelle est dénuée d'accent et donc située dans une position faible' — i.e. non-initial stem vowels are treated as unaccented/weak, with no positive statement of where accent falls.

sources.note: Short first-hand language profile; under 'Précisions linguistiques' it states that Shiwa phonology has a segmental and a suprasegmental (tonal) level and that the language has 11 vowels, 30 consonants and 5 tones (the five-tone analysis of the author's 2007/2008 mémoires: H, M, L plus rising and falling); 10 noun classes. No stress mentioned. Bibliography lists Dougère 2007, Ollomo Ella 2007 (maîtrise), Ollomo Ella 2008 (M2, with a now-dead LACITO PDF link), Puech 1989, Puech 1990.

sources.note: First-hand functionalist phonology of Shiwa. Per the author's own summary in the 2013 thesis (p.53): 32 consonant phonemes, 11 oral vowels (8 short, 3 long) and, 'sur le plan prosodique, cinq tons dont trois ponctuels (haut, moyen et bas) et deux modulés (montant et descendant)' — i.e. a five-tone analysis with a phonemic Mid, later reduced in the 2013 thesis to four tonemes (H, L, rising, falling) on three registers.
